<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our failure to perform in any of these areas could significantly weaken our competitive position, adversely affect our growth and profitability, and have a material adverse effect on our financial condition and results of operations.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<A NAME="_Toc199830665"></A><A NAME="_Toc199832887"></A><A NAME="_Toc199833554"></A><A NAME="_Toc199834626"></A><A NAME="_Toc199838185"></A><A NAME="_Toc201052231"></A><A NAME="_Toc201141649"></A><A NAME="_Toc202172877"></A><A NAME="_Toc257292278"></A><P style="margin:0px"><B><I>Consumers may decide not to use banks to complete their financial transactions, which could result in a loss of income.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Technology and other changes are allowing consumers to complete financial transactions electronically that historically have involved banks at one or both ends of the transaction. For example, consumers can now pay bills and transfer funds directly without banks. The process of eliminating banks as intermediaries, known as disintermediation, could result in the loss of fee income as well as the loss of customer deposits and income generated from those deposits. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<A NAME="_Toc257292280"></A><P style="margin:0px"><B><I>We may be adversely affected by the creditworthiness of other financial institutions.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify>Financial services institutions are interrelated as a result of trading, clearing, counterparty, or other relationships. &nbsp;We engage in transactions in the ordinary course of business with counterparties in the financial services industry, including commercial banks, brokers and dealers, investment banks and other institutional clients. &nbsp;Many of these transactions expose us to credit risk in the event of default of our counterparty or customer. &nbsp;In such instances, the collateral we hold may be insufficient to cover our </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=center>18</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=justify>losses, as we may be unable to realize upon or liquidate at prices sufficient to recover the full amount of our credit or derivative exposure. &nbsp;Such events could have a material and adverse affect on our operating results and financial condition.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<A NAME="_Toc257292281"></A><P style="margin:0px"><B><I>Uncertainty in the financial markets could result in lower fair values for securities we hold in our investment portfolio.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The upheaval in the financial markets over the past two years has adversely impacted all classes of securities and has resulted in volatility in the fair values of our investment securities. &nbsp;Issues with credit quality of the securities could result in lower fair values for these securities and may result in recognition of an other-than-temporary impairment charge, which would have a direct adverse impact on our financial condition and results of operations.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<A NAME="_Toc257292282"></A><P style="margin:0px"><B><I>Terrorism, acts of war, international conflicts and natural disasters can adversely affect us.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Acts or threats of war or terrorism, international conflicts, natural disasters, and the actions taken by the United States and other governments in response to such events, could disrupt business operations and negatively impact general business and economic conditions in the country. &nbsp;If terrorist activity, acts of war, other international hostilities or natural disasters disrupt business operations, trigger technology delays or failures, or cause damage to our physical facilities, our customers or service providers, or cause an overall economic decline, our financial condition and operating results could be materially adversely affected. &nbsp;The potential for future occurrences of these events has created many economic and political uncertainties that could adversely affect our business and results of operations in ways that we cannot presently predict. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<A NAME="_Toc257292283"></A><P style="margin:0px"><B><I>We operate in a highly regulated environment.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We are subject to extensive federal and state regulation and supervision, including regulation and supervision by Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (the &#147;Reserve Bank&#148;), FDIC and DFI. &nbsp;Existing state and federal banking laws subject us to substantial limitations with respect to loans, purchase of securities, payment of dividends and many other aspects of our business. Increased regulation of the financial institutions industry would likely increase our cost of doing business and could limit our ability to pursue business opportunities. &nbsp;There can be no assurance that future legislation or government policy will not adversely affect the banking industry in general, or our operations specifically, resulting in a competitive disadvantage. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<A NAME="_Toc257292284"></A><P style="margin:0px"><B><I>The Recent Repeal of Federal Prohibitions on Payment of Interest on Demand Deposits Could Increase our Interest Expense.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>All federal prohibitions on the ability of financial institutions to pay interest on demand deposit accounts were repealed on July&nbsp;21, 2011 as part of the Dodd-Frank Act. &nbsp;As a result, some financial institutions have commenced offering interest on demand deposits to compete for customers. &nbsp;We do not yet know what interest rates other institutions may offer as market rates begin to increase. &nbsp;Our interest expense will increase and our net interest margin will decrease if we begin offering interest on demand deposits to attract additional customers or maintain current customers, which could have a material adverse effect on our financial condition and results of operations.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B><I>We may need to raise additional capital in the future, and such capital may not be available when needed or at all.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We may need to raise additional capital in the future to provide us with sufficient capital resources and liquidity to meet our commitments and business needs, particularly if our asset quality or earnings were to deteriorate significantly. &nbsp;Our ability to raise additional capital, if needed, will depend on, among other things, conditions in the capital markets at that time, which are outside of our control, and our financial performance. &nbsp;Economic conditions and the loss of confidence in financial institutions may increase our cost of funding and limit access to certain customary sources of capital, including inter-bank borrowings, repurchase agreements and borrowings from the discount window of the Federal Reserve Board.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=center>19</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We cannot assure that such capital will be available on acceptable terms or at all. &nbsp;Any occurrence that may limit our access to the capital markets, such as a decline in the confidence of debt purchasers, depositors of the Bank or counterparties participating in the capital markets may adversely affect our capital costs and our ability to raise capital and, in turn, our liquidity. &nbsp;Moreover, if we need to raise capital in the future, we may have to do so when many other financial institutions are also seeking to raise capital and would have to compete with those institutions for investors. &nbsp;An inability to raise additional capital on acceptable terms when needed could have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B><I>Our controls and procedures may fail or be circumvented.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Management regularly reviews and updates our internal controls, disclosure controls and procedures, and corporate governance policies and procedures. &nbsp;Any system of controls, however well designed and operated, is based in part on certain assumptions and can provide only reasonable, not absolute, assurance that the objectives of the system are met. &nbsp;Any failure or circumvention of our controls and procedures or failure to comply with regulations related to controls and procedures could have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations and financial condition.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B><I>We may not be able to attract and retain skilled people.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our success depends, in large part, on our ability to attract and retain key people. &nbsp;Competition for the best people in most activities engaged in by us can be intense and we may not be able to hire people or to retain them. &nbsp;The unexpected loss of services of our key personnel could have a material adverse effect on our business because of their skills, knowledge of our market, years of industry experience and difficulty of promptly finding qualified replacement personnel.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B><I>Our information systems may experience an interruption or breach in security.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We rely heavily on communications and information systems to conduct our business. &nbsp;Any failure, interruption or breach in security of these systems could result in failures or disruptions in our customer relationship management, general ledger, deposit, loan and other systems. &nbsp;While we have policies and procedures designed to prevent or limit the effect of the failure, interruption or security breach of our information systems, there can be no assurance that any such failures, interruptions or security breaches will not occur or, if they do, that they will be adequately addressed. &nbsp;The occurrence of any failures, interruptions or security breaches of our information systems could damage our reputation, result in a loss of customer business, subject us to additional regulatory scrutiny, or expose us to civil litigation and possible financial liability any of which could have a material adverse effect on our financial condition and results of operations.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<A NAME="_Toc257292286"></A><P style="margin:0px"><B><I>Changes in the fiscal and monetary policies of the federal government and its agencies could affect the general or local economies, change the way we do business, increase our costs, or otherwise have an adverse effect on us.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify>The policies of the Federal Reserve Board impact us significantly. &nbsp;The Federal Reserve Board regulates the supply of money and credit in the United States. &nbsp;Its policies directly and indirectly influence the rate of interest earned on loans and paid on borrowings and interest-bearing deposits and can also affect the value of financial instruments we hold. &nbsp;Those policies determine to a significant extent our cost of funds for lending and investing. &nbsp;Changes in those policies are beyond our control and are difficult to predict. &nbsp;Federal Reserve Board policies can affect our borrowers, potentially increasing the risk that they may fail to repay their loans. &nbsp;For example, a tightening of the money supply by the Federal Reserve Board could reduce the demand for a borrower's products and services. &nbsp;This could adversely affect the borrower's earnings and ability to repay its loan, which could materially adversely affect us. &nbsp;</P>
<A NAME="_Toc199830673"></A><A NAME="_Toc199832895"></A><A NAME="_Toc199833562"></A><A NAME="_Toc199834634"></A><A NAME="_Toc199838193"></A><A NAME="_Toc201052239"></A><A NAME="_Toc201141656"></A><A NAME="_Toc202172884"></A><A NAME="_Toc257292288"></A><P style="margin:0px"><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=center>20</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always"><B><I>We are subject to examinations and challenges by tax authorities. </I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>In the normal course of business, we are routinely subject to examinations and challenges from federal and state tax authorities regarding the amount of taxes due in connection with investments we have made and the businesses in which we engage. &nbsp;Recently, federal and state taxing authorities have become increasingly aggressive in challenging tax positions taken by financial institutions. These tax positions may relate to tax compliance, sales and use, franchise, gross receipts, payroll, property and income tax issues, including tax base, apportionment and tax credit planning. The challenges made by tax authorities may result in adjustments to the timing or amount of taxable income or deductions or the allocation of income among tax jurisdictions. If any such challenges are made and not resolved in our favor, they could have an adverse effect on our financial condition and results of operations. <B>&nbsp;</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<A NAME="_Toc199830664"></A><A NAME="_Toc199832886"></A><A NAME="_Toc199833553"></A><A NAME="_Toc199834625"></A><A NAME="_Toc199838184"></A><A NAME="_Toc201052230"></A><A NAME="_Toc201141648"></A><A NAME="_Toc202172876"></A><A NAME="_Toc257292290"></A><P style="margin:0px"><B><I>Changes in technology may affect our operations.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The banking industry is undergoing rapid technological changes with frequent introductions of new technology-driven products and services. In addition to better serving customers, the effective use of technology increases efficiency and enables financial institutions to reduce costs. &nbsp;Our future success will depend in part on our ability to address the needs of our customers by using technology to provide products and services that will satisfy customer demands for convenience as well as create additional efficiencies in our operations. Many of our competitors have substantially greater resources to invest in technological improvements. There can be no assurance that we will be able to effectively implement new technology-driven products and services or be successful in marketing such products and services to our customers. &nbsp;Further, we rely on third- party providers to handle virtually all of the data processing aspects of our business and technological or personnel failures by these providers could also adversely our operations.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<A NAME="_Toc257292293"></A><P style="margin:0px"><B><I>We rely on dividends from the Bank for most of our revenue.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We are a separate and distinct legal entity from our subsidiary. &nbsp;We receive substantially all of our revenue from dividends from our subsidiary. &nbsp;These dividends are the principal source of funds to pay dividends to our shareholders. &nbsp;Various federal and/or state laws and regulations limit the amount of dividends the Bank may pay to us.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>In addition to such established statutory and regulatory limitations, for the foreseeable future the Bank is restricted from paying dividends on its common stock without first obtaining the consent of its banking regulators. &nbsp;These same limitations apply to us after the Reorganization. &nbsp;Further, even if we are legally able to do so, we may elect not to pay dividends on our common stock and instead decide to reinvest earnings in the Bank for operating capital and to support growth. &nbsp;See &#147;Item 5. &nbsp;Market for Registrant&#146;s Common Equity, Related Stockholder Matters and Issuer Purchases of Equity Securities &#150; Dividends and Dividend Policy.&#148;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B><I>There are numerous risks associated with our implementation of certain key strategic initiatives.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>In consultation with our banking regulators we have recently implemented or are in the process of implementing several strategic initiatives designed to strengthen our financial condition, management and strategic planning functions (see &quot;MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS &#8211; Strategic Plans and Initiatives&quot;). &nbsp;Among other things:</P>

<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=justify>Finally, one of our strategic initiatives is to achieve a Tier 1 Leverage Capital ratio of at least 9&nbsp;percent of total assets. &nbsp;However, at December&nbsp;31, 2011, our Tier 1 Leverage Capital ratio was 8.87%.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Although we believe that we may be able to increase capital to the targeted levels through internal growth and profitability, in order to accomplish these goals, we may be forced to seek additional sources of capital (including common or preferred equity, or issuing subordinated indebtedness) and may be unable to successfully do so or only be able to do so on terms which are unfavorable to us and our shareholders (including potentially having a dilutive effect on our common shareholders). &nbsp;Alternatively, we may be forced to &#147;shrink&#148; our balance sheet (reduce assets while maintaining capital levels) to improve our capital ratios, which could adversely affect us. &nbsp;Finally, if we are unable to achieve these capital goals, we may be subject to regulatory criticism and possible enforcement action against us.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Risks Associated with our Common Stock</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B><I>Our stock is illiquid.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Although our stock is publicly traded, transactions in our stock are limited and sporadic and our shareholders may not be able to readily liquidate their investment in our stock in the case of financial emergency or otherwise.<A NAME="_Toc257292295"></A></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B><I>We are effectively controlled by our directors and members of our management team.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our directors and executive officers currently beneficially own or hold the power to vote more than 19&nbsp;percent of our issued and outstanding common stock which, although it does not constitute numerical control, gives them significant influence and, in some cases, effective control over most corporate decisions to be made by our shareholders (see &#147;Security Ownership of Certain Beneficial Owners, Management and Related Shareholder Matters,&#148; Item&nbsp;12 of this Report). &nbsp;Among other things, this could, as a practical matter, limit the ability of non-management shareholders to effect a change in management or control key corporate decisions, such as amendments to the Articles of Incorporation or any merger or acquisition that is subject to shareholder approval.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B><I>An investment in our common stock is not an insured deposit.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our common stock is not a bank deposit and, therefore, is not insured against loss by the FDIC, any other deposit insurance fund or by any other public or private entity. &nbsp;Investment in our common stock is inherently risky for the reasons described in this &#147;Risk Factors&#148; section and elsewhere in this report and is subject to the same market forces that affect the price of common stock in any company. &nbsp;As a result, if you acquire our common stock, you could lose some or all of your investment.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B><I>Certain banking laws may have an anti-takeover effect.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Provisions of federal banking laws, including regulatory approval requirements, could make it more difficult for a third party to acquire us, even if doing so would be perceived to be beneficial to our shareholders. &nbsp;These provisions effectively inhibit a non-negotiated merger or other business combination, which, in turn, could adversely affect the market price of our common stock.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:48px; text-indent:-48px" align=justify><B><U>Item 2. &nbsp;Properties</U></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>As of December 31, 2011 we are operating out of two locations.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our main office is located at 2450 Witzel Avenue on the west side of Oshkosh. &nbsp;The building contains approximately 19,000 square feet on two levels. &nbsp;We own approximately 60% of the building in a </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=center>22</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=justify>condominium relationship. &nbsp;A local CPA firm owns the remaining 40%. &nbsp;The CPA firm performs payroll processing services for us, but does not perform any auditing or consulting services for us.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our branch office is a free-standing, newly constructed facility located at 2201 Jackson Street on the north side of Oshkosh that opened in January 2007. &nbsp;The building contains 3,087 square feet of floor area. &nbsp;It is a leased facility with rent of $4,116 per month. &nbsp;We are responsible for real estate taxes and utilities. &nbsp;The term of the lease is ten years, expiring in December 2016. &nbsp;The lessor is an entity owned by Director Thomas Rusch. &nbsp;Terms of the lease were reviewed by an independent appraiser, and found to be in line with current market conditions for the area. &nbsp;Lease terms were approved by the full Board of Directors, with Mr. Rusch absent from discussions. &nbsp;We believe that the properties are adequately covered by insurance and that these facilities are adequate to meet our present needs. </P>

<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Dividends and Dividend Policy</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our ability to pay dividends to our shareholders is largely dependent upon the Bank&#146;s ability to pay dividends to us. &nbsp;Historically, we have not paid cash dividends on our common stock and we do not expect to pay cash dividends on our common stock in the foreseeable future. &nbsp;We believe that it is in the best interest of our shareholders to reinvest our earnings back into our operations. &nbsp;Our dividend policy could change in the future, however, there are substantial restrictions and limitations on our ability to pay dividends.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>In connection with our implementation of certain strategic initiatives (see &quot;MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS &#150; Strategic Plans and Initiatives&quot;) our banking regulators have advised us that, for the foreseeable future, the Bank should not declare or pay dividends on its common stock without their prior consent. &nbsp;In addition to this restriction, there are a number of potential limitations that could affect the Bank&#146;s ability to pay dividends to us, and thus our ability to pay dividends to our shareholders, in the future.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The Bank's ability to pay dividends to us is regulated by various banking-related statutes. &nbsp;Under Wisconsin banking law, Wisconsin-chartered banks generally may not pay, without prior regulatory approval, dividends in excess of their net profits. &nbsp;In addition, the payment of dividends by any financial institution is affected by the requirement to maintain adequate capital pursuant to applicable capital adequacy guidelines and regulations, and a financial institution generally is prohibited from paying any dividends if, following payment thereof, the institution would be undercapitalized. &nbsp;Notwithstanding the availability of funds for dividends, however, the FDIC or the DFI may prohibit the payment of any dividends the FDIC or the WDFI&nbsp; determines such payment would constitute an unsafe or unsound practice.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Even if we may legally declare dividends, the amount and timing of such dividends will be at the discretion of our Board of Directors. &nbsp;The Board in its sole discretion may decide not to declare dividends. &nbsp;The declaration and payment of dividends will be discretionary and will depend upon operating results, financial condition, regulatory limitations, tax considerations and other factors. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We did not sell any securities without registration during 2011 or repurchase any of our common stock or other securities during the fourth quarter of 2011.</P>

<P style="margin:0px"><B>Critical Accounting Policies </B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our accounting and reporting policies are in accordance with GAAP and conform to general practices within the banking industry. &nbsp;Our significant accounting policies are described in the notes to the financial statements. &nbsp;Certain accounting policies require management to make significant estimates and assumptions, which have a material impact on the carrying value of certain assets and liabilities, and we consider these to be critical accounting policies. &nbsp;The estimates and assumptions used are based on historical experience and other factors that management believes to be reasonable under the circumstances. &nbsp;Actual results could differ significantly from these estimates and assumptions, which could have a material impact on the carrying value of assets and liabilities at the balance sheet dates and results of operations for the reporting periods. &nbsp;We believe the following critical accounting policies require the most significant estimates and assumptions that are particularly susceptible to a significant change in the preparation of our financial statements.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Income Taxes</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Deferred income taxes and liabilities are determined using the liability method. &nbsp;Under this method deferred tax assets and liabilities are determined based on the difference between the financial statement and tax bases of assets and liabilities as measured by the current enacted tax rates which will be in effect when these differences are expected to reverse. &nbsp;Provision (credit) for deferred taxes is the result of changes in the deferred tax assets and liabilities. &nbsp;A deferred tax valuation allowance is established if it is more likely than not that all or a portion of the deferred tax assets will not be realized.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We may also recognize a liability for unrecognized tax benefits from uncertain tax positions. &nbsp;Unrecognized tax benefits represent the differences between a tax position taken or expected to be taken in a tax return and the benefit recognized and measured in the financial statements. &nbsp;Interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits are classified as income taxes.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>Allowance for Loan and Lease Losses</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Management considers the policies related to the Allowance critical to the financial statement presentation. &nbsp;The Allowance represents management&#146;s assessment of the risk associated with extending credit and its evaluation of the quality of the loan portfolio. &nbsp;Management&#146;s assessment of the adequacy of the Allowance is determined based on evaluation of individual loans as well as the general risk factors inherent to the extension of credit. &nbsp;At December 31, 2011 and 2010, our allowance was 2.60% and 2.17%, respectively, of our gross loan portfolio.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>A provision for loan losses is charged to operations based on management&#146;s periodic evaluation of the factors previously mentioned, as well as other pertinent factors affecting the adequacy of the Allowance.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The following factors are considered in maintaining the Allowance:</P>

<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>These factors are evaluated at least quarterly and changes in the asset quality of individual loans will be evaluated more frequently as needed. &nbsp;We establish minimum general reserves based on the asset quality of the loan. &nbsp;General reserve factors applied to each type of loan are based upon management&#146;s experience and common industry and regulatory guidelines. &nbsp;After a loan is underwritten and booked, loans are monitored or reviewed by the account officer, management, and external loan review personnel during the life of the loan. &nbsp;Payment performance is monitored monthly for the entire loan portfolio. &nbsp;Account officers contact customers during the course of business and may be able to ascertain if weaknesses are developing with the borrower, external loan personnel perform an independent review annually, and federal and state banking regulators perform periodic reviews of the loan portfolio. &nbsp;If weaknesses develop in an individual loan relationship and are detected, the loan will be downgraded and higher reserves will be assigned based upon management&#146;s assessment of the weaknesses in the loan that may affect full collection of the debt. &nbsp;If a loan does not appear to be fully collectible as to principal and interest, the loan will be recorded as a non-accruing loan and further accrual of interest will be discontinued while previously accrued but uncollected interest is reversed against income. &nbsp;If a loan will not be collected in full, the Allowance is increased through a loan loss provision charged to earnings to reflect management&#146;s estimate of potential exposure of loss.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>In 2011, the Bank charged off approximately $0.1&nbsp;million related to two loans. &nbsp;Management elected to provide regular loan loss provisions aggregating $1.2 million in 2011 to bolster our reserves to support loan growth in 2011. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2011, the Bank had four loans classified as non-accrual. &nbsp;Three of the loans, totaling $1.0&nbsp;million, are secured by real estate. &nbsp;The remaining loan totaled $0.1&nbsp;million and is secured primarily by inventory and equipment. Management has factored these loans into the Allowance reported as of December 31, 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Management believes that resolution of these credits will be achieved without substantial additional impact to earnings. &nbsp;One of the loans listed as non-accrual totaling $0.8&nbsp;million was classified as non-accruing based on the reporting requirements of our sale of real estate. &nbsp;In March 2011, we sold a property held as Other Real Estate Owned (&#147;OREO&#148;) valued on our balance sheet at $850,000 for a total sales price of $1.2 million. &nbsp;We financed the sale under terms that defer recognition of the sale, including any gain, until sufficient loan payments are received under the installment method of accounting for sales of real estate. &nbsp;In addition, we are required to classify the loan as non-accruing until sufficient loan payments are received for conversion to full-accrual accounting. &nbsp;Management expects that the loan will convert to full-accrual status in the first quarter 2012, but there can be no assurance that it will be able to do so at that time, or ever.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Historical performance is not an indicator of future performance, particularly considering our very short operating history. &nbsp;Future results could differ materially. &nbsp;However, management believes, based upon known factors, management&#146;s judgment, and regulatory methodologies, that the current methodology used to determine the adequacy of our Allowance is reasonable.</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify>The Allowance is also subject to regulatory examinations and determinations as to adequacy, which may take into account such factors as the methodology used to calculate the Allowance and the size of the Allowance in comparison to a group of peer banks identified by the regulators. &nbsp;During their routine examinations of banks, regulatory agencies may require a bank to make additional provisions to its allowance for loan and lease losses when, in the opinion of the regulators, credit evaluations and methodology differ materially from those of management. &nbsp;While it is our policy to charge off in the </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=center>26</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=justify>current period loans for which a loss is considered probable, there are additional risks of future losses that cannot be quantified precisely or attributed to particular loans or classes of loans. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>General</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our results of operations depend primarily on net interest income, which is the difference between interest earned on interest-earning assets, such as loans and securities, and interest expense paid on interest-bearing liabilities, such as deposits and borrowed funds. &nbsp;We also generate non-interest income, such as service charges, secondary market fees for mortgage loans, and other fees. &nbsp;Non-interest expenses consist primarily of employee compensation and benefits, occupancy expenses, marketing expenses, data processing costs, and other operating expenses. &nbsp;We are subject to losses from our loan portfolio if borrowers fail to meet their obligations. &nbsp;Results of operations can also be significantly affected by general economic and competitive conditions, particularly changes in market interest rates, government policies and actions of regulatory agencies. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The following discussion focuses on the major components of our operations. &nbsp;This discussion should be read in conjunction with our financial statements and accompanying notes. &nbsp;Current performance may not be indicative of our future performance.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<A NAME="_Ref245530622"></A><P style="line-height:15pt; margin:0px; padding-left:48px; text-indent:-48px" align=justify><B>Strategic Plans and Initiatives</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The Bank, in consultation with its banking regulators, is continuing its implementation of the following strategic plans and initiatives, among others: </P>

<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>ALTHOUGH THESE STRATEGIC INITIATIVES ARE DESIGNED TO STRENGTHEN THE BANK&#146;S FINANCIAL CONDITION, MANAGEMENT AND STRATEGIC PLANNING FUNCTIONS, THERE CAN BE NO ASSURANCE THAT IT WILL BE ABLE TO IMPLEMENT THESE STRATEGIC INITIATIVES SUCCESSFULLY OR THAT IMPLEMENTING THEM WILL RESULT IN ANY IMPROVEMENTS IN OUR FINANCIAL CONDITION OR RESULTS OF OPERATIONS. &nbsp;MOREOVER, THERE ARE SIGNIFICANT RISKS ASSOCIATED WITH OUR EFFORTS TO IMPLEMENT THESE INITIATIVES OR OUR FAILURE TO IMPLEMENT THEM SUCCESSFULLY. &nbsp;SEE &#147;RISK FACTORS&#148; &nbsp;SECTION ABOVE.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>Comparisons of Operating Results for the periods ended December 31, 2011 and 2010</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We reported net income of $3.2 million for the year ended December 31, 2011, an increase of $8.3 million compared to a net loss of $5.1 million in 2010. &nbsp;Both basic and diluted income per share were $1.50 for 2011 compared to loss per share of $2.35 for 2010. &nbsp;Return on average assets and return on average equity for 2011 were 1.93% and 24.27% respectively, compared to -3.53% and -28.82%, respectively, for 2010.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We experienced improved operating results during 2011 primarily due to improved asset quality that resulted in less provision for loan loss expense relative to 2010. &nbsp;A stable loan portfolio and reduction in problem assets resulted in a $1.4 million decrease in our provision for loan losses and a $1.4 million decrease in loss on valuation of other assets for 2011 relative to 2010. &nbsp;The annual provision for loan losses was $1.2 million in 2011 compared to $2.6 million for 2010. &nbsp;We incurred a $0.1 million charge to income for the devaluation of other assets in 2011 compared to a $1.5 million valuation loss during 2010.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Comparable net income for 2011 and 2010 was significantly impacted by the accounting for income taxes related to our deferred tax asset. &nbsp;Approximately $4.0 million of the increase in net income for 2011 relative to 2010 is attributed to the impact of income tax expense. &nbsp;Income tax expense of $2.8 million was recognized in 2010 for the establishment of a full valuation allowance on our deferred tax asset. &nbsp;An income tax credit of $1.2 million was recognized in 2011 for a partial reversal of the valuation allowance based on an impairment evaluation as of December 31, 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Net interest income for 2011 was $7.0 million compared to $4.9 million during 2010. &nbsp;The $2.1&nbsp;million or 43.1% increase in net interest income relative to 2010 is attributed to the combination of growth in earning assets and the increase in net interest spread during 2011. &nbsp;Our average net interest spread and average net interest margin improved by 59 basis points and 56 basis points, respectively, from the average ratios reported for 2010.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Noninterest revenues for 2011 declined $0.5 million or 50.0% from 2010 due primarily to a decrease in rental income, as well as a decline in mortgage financing fees.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Noninterest expense for 2011 decreased $1.3 million or 23.5% from 2010 due primarily to the above noted $1.4&nbsp;million decrease in expense for devaluation of other assets.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Total assets were $175.1 million at December 31, 2011 compared to $163.7 million at December 31, 2010. &nbsp;Included in total asset growth was an increase of $18.4 million in net loans offset by a $7.1 million decrease in cash and cash equivalents compared to year-end 2010. &nbsp;Deposit growth totaled $7.4 million for 2011 and represented primarily an increase in term deposits.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>As of December 31, 2011, nonperforming loans were $1.1 million representing 0.71% of total loans. &nbsp;Nonperforming loans at December 31, 2011 include a $0.9 million loan that is classified as non-accrual </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=center>28</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=justify>based on the accounting for the financing of a purchase of bank-owned property. &nbsp;The ratio of nonperforming loans to total loans is 0.18% when this loan is excluded. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2010, nonperforming loans were $0.3 million representing 0.19% of total loans.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>As of December 31, 2011, OREO was $1.0 million representing 0.58% of total assets. &nbsp;OREO was $1.9&nbsp;million representing 1.16% of total assets at December 31, 2010. &nbsp;OREO decreased $0.9 million during 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify>The allowance for loan loss was $4.1 million, or 2.60% of total loans, at December 31, 2011 compared to an allowance of $3.0 million, or 2.17% of total loans, at December 31, 2010.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify>Our capital position remains strong with an 11.33% Tier I risk-based capital ratio for 2011. &nbsp;Our capital position, when combined with the Allowance, provides ample cushion in the event of potential loan charge-offs.</P>

<P style="margin:0px"><B>Net interest income</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Net interest income is the difference between the income earned on assets and interest paid on deposits and borrowings used to support such assets. &nbsp;Net interest income is determined by the yields earned on our interest-earning assets and the rates paid on our interest-bearing liabilities, the relative amounts of interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities, and the degree of mismatch and the maturity and repricing characteristics of our interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities. &nbsp;Net interest income divided by average interest-earning assets represents our net interest margin. &nbsp;Competition for loans and deposits has a direct effect on net interest margin.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; width:28.8px; font-size:9pt; float:left">(1)</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6px; padding-left:28.8px; text-indent:-2px; font-size:9pt" align=justify>No tax-exempt securities were held during the last three years that would affect the calculation of yield on investment securities.</P>
<P style="margin:0px; width:28.8px; font-size:9pt; clear:left; float:left">(2)</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6px; padding-left:28.8px; text-indent:-2px; font-size:9pt" align=justify>Non-accrual loans are included in the average daily loan balance, but interest income associated with these loans is recognized under the cash basis method of accounting.</P>
<P style="margin:0px; width:28.8px; font-size:9pt; clear:left; float:left">(3)</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6px; padding-left:28.8px; text-indent:-2px; font-size:9pt" align=justify>Interest rate spread is the weighted average yield on interest-earning assets minus the average rate on interest-bearing liabilities.</P>
<P style="margin:0px; width:28.8px; font-size:9pt; clear:left; float:left">(4)</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6px; padding-left:28.8px; text-indent:-2px; font-size:9pt" align=justify>Net interest margin is net interest income divided by average interest-earning assets.</P>

<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The increase in net interest income for 2011 relative to 2010 is due to the combination of growth in earning assets and the increase in net interest spread. &nbsp;Average earning assets for 2011 were $32.0 million greater than the average earning assets held during 2010. &nbsp;The growth in volume of earning assets generated $1.9&nbsp;million in additional interest income and, which when offset by $0.5&nbsp;million in interest expense tied to the growth in deposit balances, resulted in a net increase attributable to volume of $1.4&nbsp;million in net interest income for 2011 compared to 2010. &nbsp;The increase in net interest spread for 2011 relative to 2010 generated additional net interest income of $0.7&nbsp;million for 2011. &nbsp;The net interest spread for 2011 was 3.99% compared to net interest spread of 3.40% for 2010.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The improvement in net interest spread for 2011 is attributed to a reduction in cost of funds combined with an increase in yield on earning assets. &nbsp;The reduction in cost of funds during 2011 enabled the Bank to generate additional net interest income of $0.7&nbsp;million. &nbsp;The net impact of changing interest rates on net interest income contributed $0.7&nbsp;million to the increase in net interest income for 2011, including a $0.1&nbsp;million increase related to a rise in yields on earning assets.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our average interest-earning assets of $166.1 million for 2011 yielded an average return of 5.56%, compared to average interest-earning assets of $134.1 million yielding a 5.42% average return for 2010. &nbsp;The growth from 2010 to 2011 in average interest-earning asset balances totaled $32.0 million including a $32.5 million increase in average loan balances offset by a $0.5 million net decline in average balances for overnight funds and investment securities. &nbsp;Loan growth was derived from the continued expansion of the commercial loan portfolio that was first initiated with the addition of another experienced commercial lender in 2010. &nbsp;The growth in commercial loans, which typically carry a higher interest rate than investment securities, is also credited with increasing the yield on average interest-earning assets.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Interest-bearing liabilities averaged $145.1 million for 2011 with an average interest rate of 1.57%. &nbsp;The average balance and average interest rate paid on interest-bearing liabilities were $119.5 million and 2.02%, respectively, for 2010. &nbsp;The growth from 2010 to 2011 in average interest-bearing liabilities totaled $25.6 million including $6.4 million in interest-bearing demand accounts. &nbsp;The influx of lower </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>31</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>cost demand deposits combined with the repricing of term deposits in a low rate environment enabled us to decrease our cost of funds by 45 basis points during 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The Bank&#146;s net interest margin was 4.19% for 2011 compared to 3.63% for 2010. &nbsp;The 56 basis point rise in net interest margin reflects the noted improvement in funding and earning asset management for 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The increase in net interest income for 2010 relative to 2009 was attributed to growth in average earning assets of $18.5 million and an improvement in net interest spread of 82 basis points during 2010 &nbsp;over 2009. &nbsp;The growth in average earning assets from 2009 to 2010 included a $13.3 million increase in average loan balances and a $5.2 million increase in average investment assets. &nbsp;The improvement in net interest spread for 2010 was largely attributed to a 78 basis point reduction in cost of funds from 2.80% in 2009 to 2.02% in 2010. &nbsp;The decrease in cost of funds included a decline in certificates of deposit rates of 84 basis points, a decline in interest-bearing demand rates of 30 basis points, and a decline of 47 basis points in savings deposits from the prior year.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Provision for loan losses</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The provision for loan losses decreased by $1.4 million or 50.2% from $2.6 million during 2010 to $1.2 million during 2011. &nbsp;The decrease is attributed to improved asset quality that, based on management&#146;s evaluation of the adequacy of the allowance for loan losses, supported a lower provision for 2011 relative to 2010. &nbsp;During 2011, we charged off $0.1 million in loans compared to $1.8 million charged off in 2010. &nbsp;The $1.2 million annual provision for 2011, combined with a low loss experience during 2011, enabled the Bank to increase the allowance for loan losses to 2.60% of total loans as of December 31, 2011 compared to &nbsp;2.17% of total loans at December 31, 2010.</P>

<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Non-interest income decreased $0.5&nbsp;million, or 50.0%, for 2011 relative to 2010. &nbsp;A decline in rental income on OREO property had the most notable impact on non-interest income for 2011 relative to 2010, resulting from the fact that the OREO property that generated rental income in 2010 was sold in December 2010. &nbsp;The rental income for 2011 was generated on a smaller property.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>A decrease in the volume of mortgage financing activity also had an impact on non-interest income for 2011 relative to 2010. &nbsp;Secondary market fees and loan document preparation fees, which are heavily tied to mortgage financing volume, declined $84,221 and $25,236, respectively during 2011 compared to 2010.</P>

<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Non-interest expense decreased $1.3 million, or 23.5%, for 2011 relative to 2010.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Salaries and benefits increased $0.3&nbsp;million, or 12.6%, for 2011 relative to 2010. &nbsp;This increase was primarily due to staff expansion, incentive compensation, and merit-based pay increases for Bank personnel, as well as an increase in compensation expense for stock options. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Occupancy and equipment expense decreased $0.1&nbsp;million, or 14.0% for 2011 relative to 2010, attributable primarily to lower depreciation expense on computer related equipment. &nbsp;A significant amount of computer-related equipment had been fully depreciated in 2010. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Data processing expense decreased by $0.1&nbsp;million, or 28.4%, for 2011 relative to 2010. &nbsp;The renegotiation of a major vendor contract provided much of the savings reported for 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Marketing expense decreased $0.1&nbsp;million, or 51.2%, for 2011 relative to 2010. &nbsp;The overall reduction in expense is due to the reduction in formal advertising campaigns and a more focused community support initiative during 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Professional fees, which includes legal, audit, and consulting services, decreased $0.1&nbsp;million, or 14.7%, for 2011 relative to 2010. &nbsp;This was primarily attributable to a decrease in legal expense, as we had incurred additional legal expense in 2010 related to the formation of the bank holding company. &nbsp;The decrease in legal expense during 2011 was offset by additional professional fees associated with the conversion of bank stock to holding company stock and consulting fees related to an external review of bank internal controls and procedures.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>FDIC premium expense increased $0.2&nbsp;million, or 96.1%, for 2011 relative to 2010. &nbsp;The premium increase during 2011 is attributed to an increase in our assessment rate and the growth in our net assets subject to assessment.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>A $1.4&nbsp;million decrease in expense related to loss on devaluation of other assets was recognized for 2011 relative to 2010. &nbsp;The Bank reported a $0.1&nbsp;million loss on devaluation of other assets for 2011 compared to a $1.5&nbsp;million loss on devaluation reported in 2010. &nbsp;The reduction in expense is attributed to the divestment of OREO property held during 2011, combined with more stable valuations of other assets.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Total other non-interest expense decreased $0.1&nbsp;million, or 10.9%, for 2011 relative to 2010. &nbsp;The decrease in other expense is attributed to management efforts to contain overhead costs under a lean operation initiative that was implemented during 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>

<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Income Taxes</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>A $1.2&nbsp;million income tax benefit was recognized in 2011 compared to a provision for income taxes of $2.8&nbsp;million for 2010. &nbsp;The increased income taxes associated with our improved profitability in 2011 were more than offset by changes to the valuation allowance for our deferred tax asset during the year.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The basic principles for accounting for income taxes require that deferred income tax assets be analyzed to determine if a valuation allowance is required. &nbsp;A valuation allowance is required &#147;if it is more likely than not that some portion of the deferred tax asset will not be realized.&#148; </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>A valuation allowance for our deferred tax asset was established at December 31, 2010. &nbsp;In 2011, the valuation allowance was reduced by $0.8&nbsp;million for tax benefits recognized on net operating income generated during the year. &nbsp;A $1.2&nbsp;million partial reversal of the remaining valuation allowance was recognized at December 31, 2011 based on an evaluation of the continued impairment of the Bank&#146;s deferred tax asset.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>All available evidence, both positive and negative, was considered to determine whether any impairment of this asset should be recognized. &nbsp;Based on consideration of the available evidence including earnings/loss history, anticipated future pretax income, as well as the reversal period for the items giving rise to the deferred tax assets and liabilities, a partial reversal of the valuation allowance was deemed appropriate at December 31, 2011. &nbsp;The valuation allowance balance, after the partial reversal, was $1.7&nbsp;million at December 31, 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The Bank has federal and state operating loss carryforwards that approximate $1,500,000 for federal and $1,300,000 for state that may be applied against future federal and state taxable income earned. &nbsp;The carryforwards begin to expire in December 31, 2026 for federal purposes and December 31, 2021 for Wisconsin purposes.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Comparison of Financial Condition at December 31, 2011 and 2010</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Total assets at December 31, 2011 were $175.1 million, an $11.4 million increase over total assets of $163.7 million at December 31, 2010.</P>

<P style="margin:0px" align=center>34</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Total assets at December 31, 2011, were $175.1 million. &nbsp;This represents an increase of $11.4 million, or 7.0% from year-end 2010. &nbsp;Cash and cash equivalents decreased $7.1 million for 2011, including a $1.1 million decrease in cash balances and a $6.0 million decrease in federal funds sold as compared to balances held at December 31, 2010. &nbsp;Net loans increased $18.4 million, or 13.4% compared to year-end 2010. &nbsp;The loan portfolio growth is attributed to the continued expansion of the commercial loan portfolio that was first initiated with the addition of another experienced commercial lender in 2010. &nbsp;The deferred tax asset increased $1.2 million, or 100% based on the partial reversal of the valuation allowance at year-end 2011. &nbsp;Total deposits at December 31, 2011 were $7.4 million, or 4.9%, higher than year-end 2010, primarily through growth in term deposit accounts. &nbsp;Deposit growth was primarily from our local market area.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>OREO totaled $1.0 million at December 31, 2011. &nbsp;The OREO at December 31, 2011, consists of one residential property recorded at $0.8 million and two commercial real estate properties totaling $0.2 million. &nbsp;We record OREO at fair value, less cost to sell the property, with any difference between the fair value of the property and the carrying value of the loan being charged to the Allowance. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>Loans </B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our gross loans were $159.7 million at December 31, 2011 compared to $140.2 million one year earlier. &nbsp;Gross loans equaled 91.2% of total assets as of December 31, 2011, a 5.5% increase from the 85.7% reported for the previous year. &nbsp;</P>

<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>As of December 31, 2011, loan concentrations included approximately 45% of gross loans to finance commercial real estate, 25% of gross loans to finance residential property, and 18% of gross loans to finance commercial loans. &nbsp;As of &nbsp;December 31,2011, there was one individual loan relationship totaling $23.8 million or 14.9% of gross loans. &nbsp;Management does not believe that this individual loan concentration presents any additional risk of loss as the total relationship is spread over multiple types of properties and geographical locations. &nbsp;There were no other loan concentration categories that exceeded 10% as of our gross loans at December 31, 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><U>Commercial and Industrial Loans</U><I>. &nbsp;</I>Commercial and industrial loans at December&nbsp;31, 2011 totaled $28.3&nbsp;million, comprising 17.7% of our gross loans, versus $26.4&nbsp;million, or 18.8% of our gross loans at December&nbsp;31, 2010. &nbsp;We make loans to small and medium-sized businesses in our primary market area for purposes such as purchasing new, or making upgrades to, plant and equipment, inventory acquisition and various working capital purposes. &nbsp;Factors considered in making commercial loans include the borrower&#146;s cash flow, ability to repay and degree of management expertise. &nbsp;Commercial loans may be subject to many types of risks that will differ depending on the particular industry a </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>35</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>borrower is engaged in. &nbsp;General risks to an industry, or industry segment, are monitored by senior management on an ongoing basis. &nbsp;When warranted, individual borrowers who may be subject to risk due to an industry condition may be more closely analyzed and reviewed at a loan committee or board of directors&#146; level. &nbsp;On a regular basis, commercial and industrial borrowers are required to provide financial statements for our review. &nbsp;These statements are analyzed for trends and the loan is assigned a credit grade accordingly. &nbsp;Based upon this grade, the loan may receive an increased degree of scrutiny by management up to and including the requirement of additional loss reserves. &nbsp;Commercial loans will usually be secured by collateral, generally business assets that may comprise general intangibles, inventory, equipment or real estate. &nbsp;These types of collateral are subject to the risks that it will not be readily convertible into a liquid asset, if necessary, as well as risks associated with degree of specialization, mobility and general collectability in a default situation. &nbsp;To mitigate these kinds of collateral risk, we underwrite commercial loans to very strict standards, including requiring independent valuations of collateral and general acceptability based on our ability to monitor its ongoing value.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><U>Commercial Real Estate Loans</U><I>. &nbsp;</I>Commercial real estate loans totaled $71.2&nbsp;million at December&nbsp;31, 2011, comprising 44.6% of gross loans, versus $62.2&nbsp;million, or 44.4% of gross loans at December&nbsp;31, 2010. &nbsp;We make loans to borrowers secured by commercial real estate located in our market area. &nbsp;Commercial real estate lending entails certain risks not found in traditional residential real estate lending. &nbsp;Repayment is dependent upon successful management and marketing of properties and on the level of expense necessary to maintain the property. &nbsp;In underwriting this type of loan, we consider the historical and projected future cash flows from the property. &nbsp;We make an assessment of the physical condition and general location of the property securing the loan and the effect these factors will have on its future desirability from a tenant standpoint. &nbsp;We will generally lend up to a maximum 80% loan-to-value ratio and require a minimum debt service coverage ratio of 1.2 or other compensating factors. &nbsp;Repayment of these loans may be adversely affected by conditions in the real estate market or the general economy. &nbsp;Also, commercial real estate loans typically involve relatively large loan balances to a single borrower. &nbsp;To mitigate these risks, we monitor our loan concentration to make sure that they conform to our policy levels. &nbsp;Commercial real estate loans generally have a shorter maturity than other loan types, giving us the opportunity to re-price, restructure or decline to renew the loan, as appropriate. &nbsp;As with other loans, all commercial real estate loans are graded depending upon strength of credit and performance. &nbsp;A lower grade will result in increased scrutiny by management and the board of directors.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><U>Construction and Development Loans</U><I>. &nbsp;</I>Construction and development loans totaled $11.7&nbsp;million, or 7.3% of gross loans, at December 31, 2011 compared to $11.5&nbsp;million, or 8.2% of gross loans one year earlier. &nbsp;We make residential construction and development loans to customers in our market area for both speculative projects and for projects being built with end buyers already secured. &nbsp;This type of loan is subject primarily to market and general economic risk caused by inventory buildup in periods of economic prosperity. &nbsp;During times of economic stress, this type of loan has typically had a greater degree of risk than other loan types. &nbsp;To mitigate that risk, management reviews our entire construction and development portfolio on a regular basis. &nbsp;The percentage of our portfolio being built on a speculative basis is tracked very closely. &nbsp;On a quarterly basis, our portfolio is segmented by market area to allow analysis of exposure and a comparison to current inventory levels in these areas. &nbsp;Our Loan Policy also provides for limits on speculative lending on a borrower-by borrower and project-by-project basis.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><U>Residential real estate</U>. &nbsp;Residential real estate loans totaled $40.1&nbsp;million, or 25.1% of our gross loans, at December&nbsp;31, 2011 compared to $32.5 million, or 23.2% of our gross loans, and December&nbsp;31, 2010. &nbsp;Our residential real estate loans consist of residential second mortgage loans, residential construction loans and traditional mortgage lending for one-to-four family residences. &nbsp;All of our long-term fixed rate mortgages are underwritten for potential resale to the secondary market. &nbsp;We offer primarily adjustable rate mortgages. &nbsp;All loans are made in accordance with our appraisal policy, with the ratio of the loan principal to the value of collateral as established by independent appraisal not exceeding 80%, unless the borrower &#147;provides&#148; or &#147;obtains&#148; private mortgage insurance. &nbsp;We expect that these loan-to-value ratios will be sufficient to compensate for fluctuations in real estate market value and to minimize losses that could result from a downturn in the residential real estate market. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>36</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><U>Consumer Loans</U><I>. &nbsp;</I>Consumer loans, including second mortgages and home equity lines of credit, totaled $8.5&nbsp;million at December 31, 2011, comprising 5.3% of our gross loans, compared to $7.6&nbsp;million, or 5.4% of our gross loans, at December 31, 2010. &nbsp;We offer various types of consumer loans to retail customers in the communities we serve. &nbsp;These include vehicle financing, loans secured by deposits, overdraft protection lines, and secured and unsecured personal loans. &nbsp;Consumer loans are generally more risky than traditional residential real estate loans, but less risky than commercial loans. &nbsp;Risk of default is usually determined by the well being of the local economies. &nbsp;During times of economic stress, there is usually some level of job loss both nationally and locally, which directly affects the ability of the consumer to repay debt. &nbsp;We manage our risk on consumer loans by imposing limits on the debt levels that consumer borrowers may carry and on loan terms and amounts, depending upon collateral type.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:96px; text-indent:-48px" align=justify>Loans secured by deposits carry little or no risk, but the other categories of consumer loans all carry varying degrees of risk:</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify><BR></P>
<TABLE style="margin-top:0px; font-size:10pt" cellpadding=0 cellspacing=0><TR height=0 style="font-size:0"><TD width=31.2 /><TD width=48 /><TD width=492 /></TR>
<TR><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=31.2><P style="margin:0px; padding:0px">&nbsp;</P></TD><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=48><P style="margin:0px" align=justify>&#9679;</P>
</TD><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=492><P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Home equity lines carry the risk of loss in the underlying value of real estate collateral which could impact our ability to convert collateral into cash in the event of a default. &nbsp;We require our customers to carry adequate insurance coverage to pay all mortgage debt in full if the collateral is destroyed. &nbsp;</P>
</TD></TR>
<TR><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=31.2><P style="margin:0px; padding:0px">&nbsp;</P></TD><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=48><P style="margin:0px; padding:0px">&nbsp;</P></TD><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=492><P style="margin:0px; padding:0px">&nbsp;</P></TD></TR>

</TD><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=492><P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Vehicle financing presents additional risks compared to real estate lending because the collateral is declining in value over the life of the loan and is mobile. &nbsp;We attempt to manage the risks inherent in vehicle financing by matching the loan term with the age and remaining useful life of the collateral to ensure the customer always has an equity position and limit the risk of being &#147;upside down.&#148; &nbsp;Collateral is protected by requiring the customer to carry insurance that lists us as loss payee.</P>

<TR><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=31.2><P style="margin:0px; padding:0px">&nbsp;</P></TD><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=48><P style="margin:0px; padding:0px">&nbsp;</P></TD><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=492><P style="margin:0px; padding:0px">&nbsp;</P></TD></TR>

</TD><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=492><P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Secured personal loans are generally smaller and made to borrowers with somewhat limited financial resources and credit histories. &nbsp;These loans are secured by a variety of collateral with varying degrees of marketability in the event of default. &nbsp;We manage risks on these types of loans primarily at the underwriting level, with strict adherence to debt to income ratio limitations and conservative collateral valuations.</P>
</TD></TR>
<TR><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=31.2><P style="margin:0px; padding:0px">&nbsp;</P></TD><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=48><P style="margin:0px; padding:0px">&nbsp;</P></TD><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=492><P style="margin:0px; padding:0px">&nbsp;</P></TD></TR>

</TD><TD style="margin-top:0px" valign=top width=492><P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Overdraft protection lines and other unsecured personal loans carry the greatest degree of risk in our consumer lending portfolio. &nbsp;Without collateral, we are completely dependent on the commitment of the borrower to repay and the stability of the borrower&#146;s income stream. &nbsp;</P>
</TD></TR>

<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><U>Loan Participations</U>. &nbsp;We sell loan participations in the ordinary course of business when a loan we originate exceeds our legal lending limit as defined by state banking laws. &nbsp;These loan participations have been generally sold to other financial institutions without recourse. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:14px" align=justify>From time to time in the ordinary course of business we also purchase loan participations without recourse from other banks. &nbsp;Purchased loan participations are underwritten in accordance with our Loan Policy. &nbsp;Although the originating financial institution provides much of the initial underwriting documentation, we are responsible for the appropriate underwriting, approval and the ongoing evaluation of the loan. &nbsp;One risk associated with purchasing loan participations is that we often rely on information provided to us by the selling bank regarding collateral value and the borrower&#146;s capacity to pay. &nbsp;To the extent this information is not accurate, we may experience a loss on these participations. &nbsp;Otherwise, we believe that the risk related to purchased loan participations is consistent with similar loans in the portfolio. &nbsp;If a purchased loan participation defaults, we would have no direct recourse against the selling bank but will take other commercially reasonable steps to minimize our loss. &nbsp;</P>

<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Allowance for Loan Losses</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The Allowance at December 31, 2011 was $4.1&nbsp;million, compared to $3.0&nbsp;million at December&nbsp;31, 2010. &nbsp;The adequacy of the Allowance is determined based on evaluation of individual loans as well as the general risk factors inherent to all extensions of credit. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2011, our Allowance was 2.60% of our gross loan portfolio, compared to 2.17% at December 31, 2010.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The charge-off activity shown in the table below relates primarily to two loans. &nbsp;We incurred provision expense of $1.2 million during 2011 that brought the Allowance to a level management believes is adequate.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>As of December 31, 2011, we identified $7.0 million in loans subject to individual evaluation for impairment. &nbsp;We identified two loan relationships, totaling $2.2 million as impaired which required a related allowance for loan losses of $0.3&nbsp;million at year-end 2011. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2011 all impaired loans were current and performing according to agreed terms.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The Allowance represents the most significant estimate in a bank&#146;s financial statements and regulatory reports. &nbsp;Because of its significance, we realize a responsibility for developing, maintaining, and documenting a comprehensive, systematic, and consistently applied process for determining the amount of the Allowance. &nbsp;We have implemented policies and procedures to ensure that this analysis complies with GAAP and relevant supervisory guidelines.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our policies and procedures will result in an Allowance based on management&#146;s evaluation of economic conditions, volume and composition of the loan portfolio, the level of nonperforming and past due loans, and other indicators derived from reviewing the loan portfolio. &nbsp;Management will perform such reviews quarterly and adjust the level of the Allowance accordingly.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The Allowance is subject to regulatory review in the examination process to determine its adequacy. &nbsp;Regulators will take into consideration such factors as methodology used to calculate the Allowance and comparison of the Allowance level to our peers. &nbsp;Regulatory agencies, during the examination process, may require a bank to make additional provisions to their allowance for loan losses when the examiners&#146; assessment of credit evaluations and methodology differ materially from those of management. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify>Management believes that the Allowance as of December 31, 2011 was adequate to cover future losses incurred in the current loan portfolio. &nbsp;Activity in the Allowance for the years ended December 31, 2011 and 2010 are shown:</P>
