<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>40</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>At December 31, 2011, we had four loans totaling $1.1&nbsp;million classified as non-accrual. &nbsp;Three of the loans totaling $1.0&nbsp;million are secured by real estate, while the fourth $0.1&nbsp;million loan is secured by inventory and equipment. &nbsp;Management has factored these loans into the allowance at December 31, 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>One of the loans listed as non-accrual totaling $0.8&nbsp;million was classified as non-accruing based on the reporting requirements of our sale of real estate. &nbsp;In March 2011, we sold a property held as OREO valued on our balance sheet at $0.9&nbsp;million for a total sales price of $1.2 million. &nbsp;We financed the sale under terms that defer recognition of the sale, including any gain, until sufficient loan payments are received under the installment method of accounting for sales of real estate. &nbsp;In addition, we are required to classify the loan as non-accruing until sufficient loan payments are received for conversion to full-accrual accounting. &nbsp;Management expects that the loan will convert to full-accrual status in the first quarter 2012, but there can be no assurance that it will be able to do so at that time, or ever.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>For 2011, interest payments of $38,130 were received on loans classified as non-accrual. &nbsp;The amount of interest that would have been recorded as interest income had the non-accrual loans been current during the year is approximately $44,405.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>In accordance with our Loan Policy, all business purpose loans are assigned a risk rating at the time of closing. &nbsp;The scale runs from &#147;1&#148; (minimal risk) to &#147;10&#148; (loss). &nbsp;Loans are re-evaluated on a regular basis, with adjustments in the risk rating when necessary.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our Loan Policy also dictates that Loans 90 days or more delinquent and credits with risk ratings of 8, 9 or 10 that are 60 days or more delinquent be placed on non-accrual status unless the principal and interest is either secured by readily marketable securities or guaranteed by a U.S. Government agency. &nbsp;Restoration to accrual status is allowed only if principal and interest are current to terms and reasonable certainty exists as to the obligor&#146;s repayment capacity and with the approval of the Board of Directors Loan Committee.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>Investment Activities</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our Investment Policy includes strict standards regarding permissible investments, credit quality, maturity intervals and duration, and investment concentrations. &nbsp;The Asset/Liability Committee (&#147;ALCO&#148;) is responsible for making investment decisions in accordance with policies approved by our Board of Directors. &nbsp;All transactions must be made through brokers on a list approved by our Board of Directors as an addendum to the Investment Policy. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2011, our investment portfolio included U.S. government agency debt, mortgage pass-through securities, and taxable municipal bonds. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The estimated fair market value of the investment portfolio as of December 31, 2011 was $9.2&nbsp;million, including a pre-tax unrealized gain of $0.3&nbsp;million. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2010, estimated fair market value was $11.8&nbsp;million including pre-tax unrealized gain of $0.3&nbsp;million. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Our investment strategies are aimed at maximizing income, preserving principal, managing interest rate risk, and avoiding credit risk. &nbsp;Although we have no immediate plans to sell any of the securities in our portfolio, all investments are classified as &#147;available for sale.&#148; This classification allows management the flexibility to sell securities in the future to adjust the portfolio as conditions change.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="margin:0px" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>Sources of Funds</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We use deposits as the major external source of funding to finance lending and investment activities. &nbsp;In addition, we derive funds from the repayment of loans, maturities of investment securities and certificates of deposit held at other banks. &nbsp;Scheduled loan principal and interest payments and investment maturities are a relatively stable source of funds while deposit flows and loan prepayments are significantly influenced by market interest rates, economic conditions, and competition.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We offer a full line of deposit products, including checking accounts, money market accounts, savings accounts, and certificates of deposit. &nbsp;We also offer Individual Retirement Accounts (&#147;IRA&#148;) and Health Savings Accounts (&#147;HSA&#148;). &nbsp;We offer account access on-line via our web site, www.choicebank.com. &nbsp;On-line bill payment service is also available. &nbsp;Virtually all account holders reside in our primary service area. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify>We have also utilized funding from the wholesale brokered deposit market and participate in the CDARS program offered by the Promontory Interfinancial Network. &nbsp;These funding sources provide access to deposits often at lower interest rates than we must pay in our local competitive market area. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>

<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The weighted average interest rate paid on certificates of deposit for 2011 was 2.08%, compared to 2.38% paid during 2010. &nbsp;Our overall cost of funds averaged 1.57% for 2011 which was a decline of 45 basis points from the 2.02% cost of funds paid in 2010. &nbsp;The significant drop in rates reflected the lower rate environment for 2011 relative to the prior year. &nbsp;Our cost of funds was also favorably impacted by core deposit growth. &nbsp;Non interest-bearing deposits and interest-bearing demand deposits increased $1.9 million and $0.6 million, respectively during 2011. &nbsp;Non interest-bearing and interest-bearing demand deposits total 7.8% of total deposits at December 31, 2011 compared to 6.6% of total deposits at December 31, 2010.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify>We have two federal fund lines of credit totaling $12.9 million. &nbsp;The available lines of credit include $9.9 million from Bankers Bank of Madison, Wisconsin and $3.0 million from BMO Harris Bank, Milwaukee, Wisconsin. &nbsp;The line of credit at Bankers Bank is partially secured by our investment portfolio. &nbsp;The federal funds line at Bankers Bank has been used at times during the course of 2011 to fund loans and to provide liquidity. &nbsp;The federal funds line at M&amp;I Bank has not been used during 2011. &nbsp;The maximum outstanding balance at any one time under these lines during 2011 was $9.9 million and the average amount outstanding during 2011 was $1.1 million with a weighted average interest rate of 0.63%. &nbsp;At December 31, 2011 and 2010, there was no outstanding balance on our lines of credit. &nbsp;The maximum amount outstanding at any one time during 2010 was $1.8&nbsp;million and the average amount outstanding during 2010 was $0.1&nbsp;million with a weighted average interest rate of 0.65%.</P>

<P style="margin:0px"><B>Regulatory capital requirements</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We are subject to minimum capital standards as set forth by federal bank regulatory agencies. &nbsp;Our capital for regulatory purposes differs from our equity as determined under GAAP. &nbsp;Generally, &#147;Tier 1&#148; regulatory capital will equal capital as determined under generally accepted accounting principles less any unrealized gains or losses on securities available for sale while &#147;Tier 2&#148; capital includes the allowance for loan losses up to certain limitations. &nbsp;Total risk based capital is the sum of Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital. &nbsp;Our capital ratios and required minimums are shown below.</P>

<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>Liquidity</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Liquidity represents the ability to meet the needs of customers to withdraw funds from deposit accounts, to borrow funds and to meet their credit needs. &nbsp;We manage our liquidity needs in such a way that the needs of depositors and borrowers are met on a timely basis so that our operations are not interrupted. &nbsp;Sources of liquidity available to meet these needs include cash on deposit, federal funds, securities available for sale, maturities of securities and principal payments on loans. &nbsp;Growth in our deposit base provides an additional source as does access to funds through relationships with correspondent banks. &nbsp;Our liquidity needs can also be met through loan participations sold to other financial institutions. &nbsp;At December 31, 2011 and 2010 our liquidity position was considered adequate and within guidelines set forth in our liquidity policy.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>44</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>Management of the liquidity needs and requirements of the Bank is performed by our ALCO, which comprises our five senior officers. &nbsp;ALCO sets deposit prices, based on market rates and liquidity requirements. &nbsp;The loan pipeline is constantly monitored to ensure that adequate funds are available to meet commitments. &nbsp;Excess funds are invested in short-term interest-earning instruments.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:48px; text-indent:-48px" align=justify><B><U>Item 7A. &nbsp;Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk</U></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Interest Rate Sensitivity</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We are subject to interest rate risk inherent in our lending, investing, and financing activities. &nbsp;Fluctuations in market interest rates will impact both interest income and interest expense on all interest-bearing assets and interest-paying liabilities. &nbsp;Our primary objective in managing interest rate risk is to minimize any adverse impact of changes in interest rates on the net interest income while maintaining an asset/liability structure that maximizes net interest income. &nbsp;Our Asset Liability committee (&#147;ALCO&#148;) actively manages our interest rate exposure using a simulation model to measure Economic Value of Equity (&#147;EVE&#148;) and gap analysis.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>EVE is defined as the present value of the expected cash flow of assets minus the present value of expected cash flows of liabilities. &nbsp;It measures our long-term interest rate risk and identifies what the long-term effects of interest rate shocks, defined as immediate and permanent changes in rates, on our balance sheet at a point in time. &nbsp;Typical shock testing measures 100 and 200 basis points increase and decrease in rates. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The interest rate-sensitivity gap is the difference between the interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities scheduled to mature or re-price within such time period. &nbsp;A gap is considered positive when the amount of interest rate-sensitive assets exceeds the amount of interest rate-sensitive liabilities. &nbsp;A gap is considered negative when interest rate-sensitive liabilities exceed interest rate-sensitive assets. &nbsp;During a period of rising interest rates, a negative gap would tend to adversely affect net interest income, while a positive gap would tend to result in an increase in net interest income. &nbsp;Conversely, during a period of falling interest rates, a negative gap would tend to result in an increase in net interest income, while a positive gap would tend to adversely affect net interest income. &nbsp;If our assets and liabilities were equally flexible and moved concurrently, the impact of any increase or decrease in interest rates on net interest income would be minimal.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>A simple interest rate &#147;gap&#148; analysis by itself may not be an accurate indicator of how net interest income will be affected by changes in interest rates. &nbsp;Accordingly, we also evaluate how the repayment of particular assets and liabilities is impacted by changes in interest rates. &nbsp;Income associated with interest-earning assets and costs associated with interest-bearing liabilities may not be affected uniformly by changes in interest rates. &nbsp;In addition, the magnitude and duration of changes in interest rates may have a significant impact on net interest income. &nbsp;For example, although certain assets and liabilities may have similar maturities or periods of repricing, they may react in different degrees to changes in market interest rates. &nbsp;Interest rates on certain types of assets and liabilities fluctuate in advance of changes in general market rates, while interest rates on other types may lag behind changes in general market rates. &nbsp;In addition, certain assets, such as adjustable rate mortgage loans, have features (generally referred to as &#147;interest rate caps&#148;) which limit changes in interest rates. &nbsp;Prepayment and early withdrawal levels also could deviate significantly from those assumed in calculating the interest rate gap. &nbsp;The ability of many borrowers to service their debts also may decrease in the event of an interest rate increase.</P>

<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60.467px; padding-right:57.6px" align=justify>Adjustable rate loans are included in the period in which their interest rates are scheduled to adjust. &nbsp;Fixed rate loans are included in the periods in which they are anticipated to be repaid based on scheduled maturities. &nbsp;Investment securities are included in their period of maturity while mortgage-backed securities are included according to expected repayment. &nbsp;Certificates of deposit are presented according to contractual maturity. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60.467px; padding-right:57.6px" align=justify>As shown above, as of December 31, 2011, we are highly liability sensitive over the next twelve month period. That means that our interest rate spread would decrease if rates rise during that period.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60.467px; padding-right:57.6px" align=justify>It is important to note that about $30.9 million of loans re-pricing are tied to an index (generally 30-day LIBOR or Wall Street Prime) and would automatically reprice if and as those rates change. &nbsp;About 64.3% of repricing loans tied to an index are at their contractual floor rates and would not adjust downward if the related index rate should decline. &nbsp;There is also the potential that some repricing loans that are at their contractual floor rates would not adjust upward if the repricing rate tied to an increase in the related index rate remains below the existing floor rate. &nbsp;In short, while repricing loans that are tied to an index automatically reprice as the index rate changes, those loans at their floor rate may not reprice or may not reprice to the same extent as the change in the related index rate.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60.467px; padding-right:57.6px" align=justify>The rates we pay on our interest-bearing liabilities (primarily deposits), on the other hand, are not tied to an index, but are adjusted by management based on local market rates, need for funds, and other considerations, such that the rates of interest we pay are somewhat within our control and typically do not re-price as quickly or dramatically as loans.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:14pt">Note 1: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:11pt"><B>Organization</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Choice Bancorp (the &#147;Company&#148;) is a bank holding company as defined in the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956, as amended. &nbsp;As such, it exercises control over Choice Bank (the &#147;Bank&#148;).</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Choice Bank is a full-service community-oriented commercial bank. &nbsp;The Bank offers a broad range of commercial and consumer banking services to local businesses, professionals, community service organizations, and individuals. &nbsp;The Bank commenced operations in July 2006. &nbsp;The Bank operates with two locations in Oshkosh, Wisconsin. &nbsp;The Bank is subject to the regulations of certain federal and state agencies and undergoes periodic examinations by those regulatory authorities.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:11pt"><B>Basis of Consolidation</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of Choice Bancorp, Inc. and its subsidiary. &nbsp;All intercompany balances and transactions have been eliminated in consolidation.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:11pt"><B>Use of Estimates in Preparation of Financial Statements</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The preparation of the accompanying consolidated financial statements in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities, the disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial statements, and the reported amounts of revenue and expenses during the reporting period. &nbsp;Actual results may differ from these estimates.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:11pt"><B>Cash and Cash Equivalents</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>For purposes of reporting cash flows in the consolidated financial statements, cash and cash equivalents include cash on hand, interest-bearing and non-interest-bearing accounts in other financial institutions, and federal funds sold, all of which have original maturities of three months or less.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Securities</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Securities are classified as available for sale and are carried at fair value, with unrealized gains and losses reported in accumulated other comprehensive income. &nbsp;Amortization of premiums and accretion of discounts are recognized in interest income using the interest method over the estimated lives of the securities.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:57.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Declines in fair value of securities that are deemed to be other-than-temporary, if applicable, are reflected in earnings as realized losses. &nbsp;In estimating other-than-temporary impairment losses, management considers the length of time and the extent to which fair value has been less than cost, the financial condition and near-term prospects of the issuer, and the intent and ability of the Company to retain its investment in the issuer for a period of time sufficient to allow for any anticipated recovery in fair value. &nbsp;Gains and losses on the sale of securities are recorded on the trade date and determined using the specific-identification method.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Loans Held for Sale</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Loans originated and intended for sale in the secondary market are carried at the lower of cost or estimated fair value in the aggregate. &nbsp;Net unrealized losses, if any, are recognized through a valuation allowance by charges to income.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Rate Lock Commitments</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Company enters into commitments to originate loans whereby the interest rate on the loan is determined prior to funding (rate lock commitments). &nbsp;Rate lock commitments on mortgage loans that are intended to be sold are considered to be derivatives. &nbsp;Rate lock commitments are recorded only to the extent of fees received since recording the estimated fair value of these commitments would not have a significant impact on the financial statements.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Loans</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Loans that management has the intent and ability to hold for the foreseeable future or until maturity or payoff generally are reported at their outstanding unpaid principal balances adjusted for charge-offs and the allowance for loan losses. &nbsp;Interest on loans is accrued and credited to income based on the unpaid principal balance.</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The accrual of interest on loans is discontinued when, in the opinion of management, there is an indication the borrower may be unable to make payments as they become due. &nbsp;When loans are placed on nonaccrual or charged off, all unpaid accrued interest is reversed against interest income. &nbsp;The interest on these loans is subsequently accounted for on the cash basis until qualifying for return to accrual. &nbsp;Loans are returned to accrual status when all the principal and interest amounts contractually due are brought current and future payments are reasonably assured.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Allowance for Loan Losses</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The allowance for loan losses is established through a provision for loan losses charged to expense as losses are estimated to have occurred. &nbsp;Loan losses are charged against the allowance when management believes that the collectability of the principal is unlikely. &nbsp;Subsequent recoveries, if any, are credited to the allowance.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Management regularly evaluates the allowance for loan losses using the Company's past loan loss experience, known and inherent risks in the portfolio, composition of the portfolio, adverse situations that may affect the borrower's ability to repay, estimated value of any underlying collateral, current economic conditions, and other relevant factors. &nbsp;This evaluation is inherently subjective since it requires material estimates that may be susceptible to significant change.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The allowance for loan losses consists of specific, general, and unallocated components. &nbsp;The specific component relates to loans that are classified as doubtful, substandard, or special mention and includes allowances estimated for impaired loans. &nbsp;The general component covers nonclassified loans and is based on historical loss experience adjusted for qualitative factors. &nbsp;An </P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:45.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Allowance for loan losses (Continued)</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>unallocated component is maintained to cover uncertainties that could affect management's estimate of probable losses and reflects the margin of imprecision inherent in the underlying assumptions used in the methodologies for estimating specific and general losses in the portfolio.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:45.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The allowance for loan losses includes specific allowances related to loans that have been judged to be impaired under current accounting standards. &nbsp;A loan is impaired when, based on current information, it is probable that the Company will not collect all amounts due in accordance with the contractual terms of the loan agreement. &nbsp;Management determines whether a loan is impaired on a case-by-case basis, taking into consideration the payment status, collateral value, length and reason of any payment delays, the borrower's prior payment record, and any other relevant factors. &nbsp;Large groups of smaller balance homogeneous loans, such as residential mortgage and consumer loans, are collectively evaluated in the allowance for loan losses analysis and are not subject to impairment analysis unless such loans have been subject to a restructuring agreement. &nbsp;Specific allowances for impaired loans are based on discounted cash flows of expected future payments using the loan's initial effective interest rate or the fair value of the collateral if the loan is collateral dependent.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:45.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>In addition, various regulatory agencies periodically review the allowance for loan losses. &nbsp;These agencies may require additions to the allowance for loan losses based on their judgments of collectability.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:45.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Premises and Equipment</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:45.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Land is carried at cost. &nbsp;Premises and equipment are stated at cost less accumulated depreciation computed on the straight-line method over the estimated useful lives of the assets.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:45.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Other Real Estate Owned</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:45.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Assets acquired through, or in lieu of, loan foreclosures are held for sale and are initially recorded at fair value at the date of foreclosure, establishing a new cost basis. &nbsp;Subsequent to foreclosure, valuations are periodically performed by management, and the assets are carried at the lower of carrying amount or fair value less cost to sell. &nbsp;Revenue and expenses from operations related to other real estate owned are charged to expense. Changes in the valuation allowance are included in losses on OREO and other investments.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:45.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Stock Compensation Plans</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:45.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Company accounts for employee stock compensation plans using the fair value based method of accounting. &nbsp;Compensation expense is recognized based on the fair value of unvested stock options and awards over the requisite service period.</P>

<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:45.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Advertising costs are expensed as incurred and recorded as marketing expense, a component of noninterest expense.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:39.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Income Taxes</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:39.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Deferred income tax assets and liabilities have been determined using the liability method. &nbsp;Deferred tax assets and liabilities are determined based on the difference between the financial statement and tax bases of assets and liabilities as measured by the current enacted tax rates which will be in effect when these differences are expected to reverse. &nbsp;Provision (credit) for deferred taxes is the result of changes in the deferred tax assets and liabilities. &nbsp;A deferred tax valuation allowance is established if it is more likely than not that all or a portion of the deferred tax assets will not be realized. The Company may also recognize a liability for unrecognized tax benefits from uncertain tax positions. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:39.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Unrecognized tax benefits represent the differences between a tax position taken or expected to be taken in a tax return and the benefit recognized and measured in the financial statements. &nbsp;Interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits are classified as income taxes.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:39.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Off-Balance-Sheet Financial Instruments</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:39.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>In the ordinary course of business, the Company has entered into off-balance-sheet financial instruments including commitments to extend credit and unfunded commitments under lines of credit. &nbsp;Such financial instruments are recorded in the financial statements when they become payable.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:39.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Comprehensive Income (Loss)</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:39.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Comprehensive income (loss) is shown on the statements of stockholders' equity. &nbsp;Comprehensive income (loss) consists of net income (loss) and other comprehensive income. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s accumulated other comprehensive income is comprised of the unrealized gains on securities available for sale, net of tax, and is shown on the statements of stockholders' equity.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:39.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Earnings (Loss) per Share</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:39.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Basic earnings (loss) per share represents operating income (losses) divided by the weighted average number of common shares outstanding during the period. &nbsp;Due to a weighted average strike price of potential common shares outstanding which is higher than the estimated average market value of the Company's common stock, anti-dilution would occur in calculating diluted earnings per share. &nbsp;As such, diluted earnings per share is not presented.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:39.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>New Accounting Pronouncements</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:39.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>ASU No. 2011-02, &#147;Receivables (Topic 310) - A Creditor&#146;s Determination of Whether a Restructuring Is a Troubled Debt Restructuring.&#148; ASU No. 2011-02 clarifies which loan modifications constitute troubled debt restructurings and is intended to assist creditors in determining whether a modification of the terms of a receivable meets the criteria to be considered a troubled debt restructuring, both for purposes of recording an impairment loss and for disclosure of troubled debt restructurings. In evaluating whether a restructuring constitutes a troubled debt restructuring, a creditor must separately conclude, under the guidance clarified by ASU No. 2011-02, that both of the following exist: (a) the restructuring constitutes a concession; and (b) the debtor is experiencing financial difficulties. ASU No. 2011-02 became effective for the Company on July 1, 2011, and applies retrospectively to restructurings occurring on or after January 1, 2011. &nbsp;The adoption of this guidance did not have any impact on the Company&#146;s consolidated statement of income, its consolidated balance sheet, or its consolidated statement of cash flows.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:33.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>ASU No. 2011-03, &#147;Transfers and Servicing (Topic 860) - Reconsideration of Effective Control for Repurchase Agreements.&#148; ASU No. 2011-03 is intended to improve financial reporting of repurchase agreements and other agreements that both entitle and obligate a transferor to repurchase or redeem financial assets before their maturity. ASU No. 2011-03 removes from the assessment of effective control (i) the criterion requiring the transferor to have the ability to repurchase or redeem the financial assets on substantially the agreed terms, even in the event of default by the transferee, and (ii) the collateral maintenance guidance related to that criterion. ASU No. 2011-03 will be effective for the Company on January 1, 2012 and is not expected to have a significant impact on the Company&#146;s financial statements.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:33.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>ASU No. 2011-04, &#147;Fair Value Measurement (Topic 820) - Amendments to Achieve Common Fair Value Measurements and Disclosure Requirements in U.S. GAAP and IFRSs.&#148; ASU No. 2011-04 amends Topic 820, &#147;Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures,&#148; to converge the fair value measurement guidance in U.S. generally accepted accounting principles and International Financial Reporting Standards. ASU No. 2011-04 clarifies the application of existing fair value measurement requirements, changes certain principles in Topic 820 and requires additional fair value disclosures. ASU No. 2011-04 is effective for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2011, and is not expected to have a significant impact on the Company&#146;s financial statements.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:33.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>ASU No. 2011-05, &#147;Comprehensive Income (Topic 220) - Presentation of Comprehensive Income.&#148; ASU No. 2011-05 amends Topic 220, &#147;Comprehensive Income,&#148; to allow an entity the option to present the total of comprehensive income, the components of net income, and the components of other comprehensive income in either a single continuous statement of comprehensive income or in two separate but consecutive statements. Additionally, ASU No. 2011-05 requires entities to present, on the face of the financial statements, reclassification adjustments for items that are reclassified from other comprehensive income to net income in the statement or statements where the components of net income and the components of other comprehensive income are presented. The option to present components of other comprehensive income as part of the statement of changes in stockholders&#146; equity was eliminated. ASU No. 2011-05 is effective for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2011, and is not expected to have a significant impact on the Company&#146;s financial statements. </P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:27.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>New Accounting Pronouncements (Continued)</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:33.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>ASU No. 2011-08, &#147;Intangibles - Goodwill and Other (Topic 350) - Testing Goodwill for Impairment.&#148; ASU No. 2011-08 amends Topic 350, &#147;Intangibles &#150; Goodwill and Other,&#148; to give entities the option to first assess qualitative factors to determine whether the existence of events or circumstances leads to a determination that it is more likely than not that the fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying amount. If, after assessing the totality of events or circumstances, an entity determines it is not more likely than not that the fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying amount, then performing the two-step impairment test is unnecessary. However, if an entity concludes otherwise, then it is required to perform the first step of the two-step impairment test by calculating the fair value of the reporting unit and comparing the fair value with the carrying amount of the reporting unit. ASU No. 2011-08 is effective for annual and interim impairment tests beginning after December 15, 2011, and is not expected to have any impact on the Company&#146;s financial statements.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:27.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>ASU No. 2011-10, Derecognition of In Substance Real Estate &#150; A Scope Clarification. &nbsp;This update to Topic 360, &#147;Property, Plant and Equipment,&#148; requires that a parent (reporting entity) ceases to have a controlling financial interest in a subsidiary that is in substance real estate as a result of default on the subsidiary&#146;s nonrecourse debt, the reporting entity should apply the guidance in Subtopic 360-20 to determine whether it should derecognize the in substance real estate. The amendments are effective for fiscal years, and interim periods, within those years, beginning on or after June 15, 2012. Early adoption is permitted. The adoption of ASU No. 2011-10 will have no impact on the Company&#146;s financial statements.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:27.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>ASU No. 2011-11, Disclosures About Offsetting Assets and Liabilities. The updates to Topic 210, &#147;Balance Sheet,&#148; require an entity to disclose information about offsetting and related arrangements to enable users of its financial statements to understand the effect of those arrangements on its financial position. Entities are required to disclose both gross information and net information about both instruments and transactions eligible for offset in the statement of financial position and instruments and transactions subject to an agreement similar to a master netting arrangement. This scope would include derivatives, sale and repurchase agreements and reverse sale and repurchase agreements, and securities borrowing and securities lending arrangements. An entity is required to apply the amendments for annual reporting periods beginning on or after January 1, 2013, and interim periods within those annual periods. An entity should provide the disclosures required by those amendments retrospectively for all comparative periods presented. The adoption of ASU No. 2011-11 is not expected to have a material impact on the Company&#146;s financial statements.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:27.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Reclassifications</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:27.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Certain reclassifications have been made to the 2010 financial statements to conform to the 2011 classifications.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:14pt">Note 2: Cash and Due From Banks</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:60px; padding-right:51.6px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>In the normal course of business, the Company maintains cash and due from bank balances with correspondent banks in non-interest bearing transaction accounts. &nbsp;Consequently, all account balances with correspondent banks are guaranteed by the FDIC through January 1, 2013, upon which time the insurance is expected to revert back to $250,000.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="margin:0px; font-size:14pt">Note 4: Loans (Continued)</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Company analyzes loans individually by classifying the loans as to credit risk. &nbsp;The Company categorizes business purpose loans into risk categories based on relevant information about the ability of borrowers to service their debt such as: current financial information, historical payment experience, credit documentation, public information, and current economic trends, among other factors. &nbsp;Non-business loans are analyzed and categorized as performing or non-performing.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Company uses the following definitions for risk ratings when classifying business purpose loans:</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Risk Grade 1 &#150; Superior</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Business purpose loans rated &#147;1&#148; are characterized by borrowers fully responsible for the loan with excellent capacity to pay principal and interest. &nbsp;Loans rated &#147;1&#148; may be secured by readily marketable collateral.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Risk Grade 2 &#150; Minimal</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Business purpose loans rated &#147;2&#148; are characterized by borrowers consistently capable of generating industry margins, profits, and cash-flow, regardless of economic or business conditions.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Risk Grade 3 &#150; Low</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Business purpose loans rated &#147;3&#148; are characterized by borrowers well established in a market and/or industry, capable of generating above average margins, profits, and cash-flow in most economic or business conditions.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Risk Grade 4 &#150; Modest</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Business purpose loans rated &#147;4&#148; are characterized by borrowers established in specific markets or industries in satisfactory condition. &nbsp;Profit margin, profitability, and cash flow trends are positive but not consistently stable.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Risk Grade 5 &#150; Average</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Business purpose loans rated &#147;5&#148; are characterized by borrowers operating in relatively stable industries but susceptible to moderate cyclicality, unfavorable changes in the economy, or competitive influences. &nbsp;These loans are characterized by average asset quality, limited liquidity, and tighter debt service coverage.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Risk Grade 6 &#150; Acceptable</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Business purpose loans rated &#147;6&#148; are characterized by borrowers that are potentially weak that deserve management&#146;s close attention. &nbsp;Potential weaknesses, if left uncorrected, may result in deterioration of the repayment prospects for the asset or inadequately protect the Company&#146;s credit position at some future date.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Risk Grade 7 &#150; Watch</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Business purpose loans rated &#147;7&#148; are characterized by borrowers that warrant greater monitoring due to financial condition or unresolved and identified risk factors.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Risk Grade 8 &#150; Problem</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Business purpose loans rated &#147;8&#148; include loans inadequately protected by the current net worth and paying capacity of the borrower or of the collateral pledged, if any. &nbsp;Loans so classified have a well-defined weakness or weaknesses that jeopardize the liquidation of the debt. &nbsp;Problem loans are characterized by the distinct possibility that the Company will sustain some loss if the deficiencies are not corrected.</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR>

<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:15.533px; font-size:14pt">Note 4: Loans (Continued)</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Non-Business Purpose Loans</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Non-business purpose loans are analyzed on a pass or fail basis. &nbsp;These loans are presented either as performing or non-performing, separately from risk-graded loans. &nbsp;See below for a description of non-performing loans. &nbsp;All other non-business purpose loans are classified as performing.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Non-Performing Loans</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Loans are reported as non-performing when principal or interest has been in default for a period of ninety-days or more or if the collection of interest is in question. &nbsp;Both business purpose and non-business purpose loans are included in this category as appropriate. &nbsp;Business purpose loans that are classified as non-performing are presented together with non-business purpose loans that are classified as non-performing, and separately from their risk-grade category.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="margin:0px; font-size:14pt">Note 7: Borrowed Funds</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Borrowed funds included notes payable of $290,000 at December 31, 2011. &nbsp;The Company obtained a $290,000 line of credit from certain of its directors by issuing and selling to such directors $290,000 of promissory notes. &nbsp;The Director Notes were issued in response to the Banking Regulators&#146; condition to their approval of the Reorganization that the Company obtain financing sufficient to enable it to reimburse the Bank for certain expenses of the Reorganization and pay its ongoing holding company-only expenses.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Director Notes have a fixed interest rate of 6.00% and mature on March 10, 2014. &nbsp;The Director Notes are unsecured obligations of the Company and interest on the notes is payable at maturity.</P>

<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:14pt">Note 8: Income Taxes (Continued)</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Deferred income taxes are provided for the temporary differences between the financial reporting basis and the tax basis of the Bank&#146;s assets and liabilities.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>A valuation allowance for the Bank&#146;s deferred tax asset was established at December 31, 2010. &nbsp;In 2011, the valuation allowance was reduced by $805,200 for tax benefits recognized on net operating income generated during the year. &nbsp;A $1,200,000 partial reversal of the remaining valuation allowance was recognized at December 31, 2011 based on an evaluation of the ability of the Company to recognize its net deferred tax assets.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>All available evidence, both positive and negative, was considered to determine whether any impairment of this asset should be recognized. &nbsp;Based on consideration of the available evidence including earnings/loss history, anticipated future pretax income, as well as the reversal period for the items giving rise to the deferred tax assets and liabilities, a partial reversal of the valuation allowance was deemed appropriate at December 31, 2011. &nbsp;The valuation allowance balance, after the partial reversal, was $1,655,200 at December 31, 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:14pt">Note 8: Income Taxes (Continued)</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Company has federal and state operating loss carryforwards that approximate $1,500,000 for federal and $1,300,000 for state that may be applied against future federal and state taxable income earned. &nbsp;The carryforwards begin to expire in December 31, 2026, for federal purposes and December 31, 2021, for Wisconsin purposes.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Income tax returns for the calendar years 2007 through 2010, with few exceptions, remain open to examination by federal and state taxing authorities.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:14pt">Note 9: Stockholders&#146; Equity and Regulatory Matters</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The declaration and payment of cash dividends by the Company to stockholders is restricted by certain statutory and regulatory limitations. &nbsp;These limitations state that the Company may not declare or pay a dividend if the total of all dividends declared during the calendar year, including the proposed dividend, exceeds the sum of the Company's net income during the current calendar year and the retained net income of the prior two calendar years. &nbsp;Prior written regulatory approval must be obtained to make an exception. &nbsp;There were no cash dividends paid to stockholders by the Company in 2011 or 2010.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Bank is subject to various regulatory capital requirements administered by federal and state banking agencies. &nbsp;Failure to meet minimum capital requirements can initiate certain mandatory and possibly additional discretionary, actions by regulators that, if undertaken, could have a direct material effect on the Bank's financial statements. &nbsp;Under capital adequacy guidelines and the regulatory framework for prompt corrective action, the Bank must meet specific capital guidelines that involve quantitative measures of assets, liabilities, and certain off-balance-sheet items as calculated under regulatory accounting practices. &nbsp;The capital amounts and classification are also subject to qualitative judgments by the regulators about components, risk weightings, and other factors.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Quantitative measures established by regulation to ensure capital adequacy require the Bank to maintain minimum amounts and ratios (set forth in the table below) of total and Tier I capital to risk-weighted assets, and of Tier I capital to average assets. &nbsp;It is management's opinion, as of December 31, 2011, that the Bank meets all applicable capital adequacy requirements.</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>As of December 31, 2011, the most recent notification from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation categorized the Bank as well capitalized under the regulatory framework for prompt corrective action. &nbsp;To be categorized as well capitalized, the Bank must maintain minimum total risk-based, Tier I risk-based, and Tier I leverage ratios as set forth in the table.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:14pt" align=justify>Note 9: Stockholders&#146; Equity and Regulatory Matters (Continued)</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>In consultation with its banking regulators, the Bank has recently implemented several strategic initiatives designed to strengthen its financial condition. One of its strategic initiatives is to achieve a Tier 1 Leverage Capital ratio of at least 8% of total assets and a Total Risk-Based Capital ratio level of at least 11 percent of total assets by May 23, 2011 and a Tier 1 Leverage Capital ratio of 9% and Total Risk-Based Capital ratio of 12% by August&nbsp;21, 2011. &nbsp;At December 31, 2011, the Bank&#146;s Tier 1 Leverage Capital ratio was 8.87% and its Total Risk-Based Capital ratio was 12.61%. &nbsp;The Bank continues to pursue strategies to enhance its capital position in an effort to achieve the levels established pursuant to the initiative indicated above.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-53.733px; font-size:14pt">Note 10: Commitments, Contingencies, and Credit Risk</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Financial Instruments With Off-Balance-Sheet Credit Risk</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Company is a party to financial instruments with off-balance-sheet risk in the normal course of business to meet the financing needs of its customers. &nbsp;These instruments involve, to varying degrees, elements of credit risk in excess of the amount recognized in the balance sheets.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Company's exposure to credit loss is represented by the contractual, or notional, amount of these commitments. &nbsp;The Company follows the same credit policies in making commitments as it does for on-balance-sheet instruments. &nbsp;Since some of the commitments are expected to expire without being drawn upon and some of the commitments may not be drawn upon to the total extent of the commitment, the notional amount of these commitments does not necessarily represent future cash requirements.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The following commitments were outstanding at December 31:</P>

<P style="margin:0px" align=center><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Commitments to extend credit are agreements to lend to a customer at fixed or variable rates as long as there is no violation of any condition established in the contract. &nbsp;Commitments generally have fixed expiration dates or other termination clauses and may require payment of a fee. &nbsp;The amount of collateral obtained upon extension of credit is based on management's credit evaluation of the customer.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Unfunded commitments under commercial lines of credit, home equity lines of credit, and overdraft protection agreements are commitments for possible future extensions of credit to existing customers. &nbsp;These lines of credit may or may not require collateral and may or may not contain a specific maturity date. &nbsp;Commitments for equity lines of credit may expire without being drawn upon. &nbsp;Therefore, the total commitments do not necessarily represent future cash requirements.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="margin:0px; font-size:14pt">Note 10: Commitments, Contingencies, and Credit Risk (Continued)</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Legal Contingencies</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Various legal claims arise from time to time in the normal course of business. &nbsp;In the opinion of management, any liability resulting from such proceedings would not have a material impact on the financial statements.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Concentration of Credit Risk</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The majority of the Company's loans, commitments, and standby letters of credit have been granted to customers in the Company's market area. &nbsp;The concentrations of credit by type are set forth in Note 4. &nbsp;Standby letters of credit were granted primarily to commercial borrowers. &nbsp;Management believes the diversity of the local economy will prevent significant losses during the economic downturn, but the portfolio is monitored on a continuous basis.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><B>Unused Lines of Credit</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>As of December 31, 2011, the Company has unused lines of credit of $12,900,000. &nbsp;The available lines of credit include $9,900,000 at Bankers' Bank, Madison and $3,000,000 at BMO Harris Bank, Milwaukee. &nbsp;The maximum outstanding at any one time during 2011 was $9.9 million. &nbsp;The weighted rate on average outstanding balances for 2011 was 0.64%. &nbsp;At December 31, 2011, there was no outstanding balance on the Company&#146;s lines of credit.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:14pt" align=justify>Note 11: Employee Benefit Plan</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Company sponsors a 401(k) profit sharing plan covering substantially all employees. &nbsp;Employees are allowed to make voluntary contributions to the plan up to 15% of their compensation, subject to limits imposed by federal tax laws.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>During 2011 and 2010, the Company made matching contributions on behalf of each employee participant. &nbsp;The Company contributed an amount equal to 100% of the amount of each employee elective contribution that did not exceed 3% of the employee participant&#146;s compensation and 50% of the amount of the employee participant&#146;s contribution that exceeded 3% of the employee participant&#146;s compensation up to a maximum Company contribution of 4% of the employee participant&#146;s compensation.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Company expensed contributions of $56,791 for 2011 and expensed contributions of $60,001 for 2010.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-53.733px; font-size:14pt">Note 12: Stock Compensation Plan</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:17.6px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Choice Bank Stock Option Plan was approved by shareholders on July 11, 2006 and adopted by the Company on the Reorganization Date. &nbsp;The Board of Directors reserved 360,000 shares of Company stock for use as option awards to employees and directors under the Plan. &nbsp;The exercise price equals the market value of the Bank's stock at the grant date. &nbsp;The vesting period ranges from one to three years, and the maximum term is ten years.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:17.6px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Compensation cost relates to share-based payment transactions being recognized in the financial statements with measurement based on the fair value of the equity instrument at time of grant. &nbsp;For the years ended December 31, 2011 and 2010, the Company recognized $137,751 and $11,028, respectively, in compensation expense for stock options. &nbsp;139,000 stock options were granted in 2011 of which 42,500 vested on the grant date and 96,500 that will vest proportionately over a period of three years. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2011 there were 151,000 shares available to be granted under the Company Stock Option Plan.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:14pt" align=justify>Note 13: Warrants</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-53.733px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Company has two types of warrants outstanding to purchase shares of common stock at December 31, 2011. &nbsp;Initial shareholders in the Bank received warrants to purchase one share of common stock for every five shares of common stock purchased in the Bank&#146;s initial common stock offering (&#147;shareholder warrants&#148;). &nbsp;A total of 431,990 shareholder warrants were issued. &nbsp;Originally, the shareholder warrants were exercisable at a price of $12.50 per share at any time until July 24, 2009. &nbsp;On October 28, 2008, the Board of Directors extended the expiration date to July 24, 2012. &nbsp;As part of the Reorganization Transaction, shareholder warrants to purchase Bank stock were converted into warrants to purchase Company stock at the same price. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2011, 620 shareholder warrants had been exercised and 431,370 shareholder warrants remained outstanding.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-53.733px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Bank&#146;s organizers advanced funds and guaranteed loans for organizational and other pre-opening expenses. As consideration for the financial risk assumed, the organizers received warrants to purchase one share of common stock for every $10 placed at risk, up to a maximum of 11,250 warrants per organizer (&#147;organizer warrants&#148;). &nbsp;A total of 213,750 organizer warrants have been issued. The organizer warrants are exercisable at a price of $10.00 per share at any time until July 24, 2016. The organizer warrants were accounted for in accordance with the fair value method and recognized as stock compensation included in start-up expenses at July 24, 2006. As part of the Reorganization Transaction, organizer warrants to purchase Bank stock were converted into warrants to purchase Company stock at the same price. &nbsp;None of the organizer warrants had been exercised as of December 31, 2011.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:14pt" align=justify>Note 15: Fair Value Measurements</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-53.733px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Accounting standards describe three levels of inputs that may be used to measure fair value (the fair value hierarchy). &nbsp;The level of an asset or liability within the fair value hierarchy is based on the lowest level of input significant to the fair value measurement of that asset or liability.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-53.733px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Following is a brief description of each level of the fair value hierarchy:</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-24px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Level-1 - Fair value measurement is based on quoted prices for identical assets or liabilities in active markets.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-24px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Level-2 - Fair value measurement is based on: (1) quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in active markets; (2) quoted prices for identical or similar assets or liabilities in markets that are not active; or (3) valuation models and methodologies for which all significant assumptions are or can be corroborated by observable market data.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-24px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Level-3 - Fair value measurement is based on valuation models and methodologies that incorporate at least one significant assumption that cannot be corroborated by observable market data. &nbsp;Level 3 measurements reflect the Bank's estimates about assumptions market participants would use in measuring fair value of the asset or liability.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-53.733px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Some assets and liabilities, such as securities available for sale, are measured at fair value on a recurring basis under accounting principles generally accepted in the United States. &nbsp;Other assets and liabilities, such as impaired loans, may be measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-53.733px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Following is a description of the valuation methodology used for each asset and liability measured at fair value on a recurring or nonrecurring basis, as well as the classification of the asset or liability within the fair value hierarchy.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-53.733px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Securities available for sale</I> - Securities available for sale are classified as Level 2 measurements within the fair value hierarchy. &nbsp;Level 2 securities include U.S. government and agency securities, obligations of states and political subdivisions, corporate debt securities, and mortgage-related securities. &nbsp;The fair value measurement of a Level 2 security is obtained from an independent pricing service and is based on recent sales of similar securities and other observable market data.</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>82</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-56px; font-size:18pt">Choice Bancorp, Inc.</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-56px; font-size:14pt">Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements</P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-bottom:4px; border-bottom:2px solid #000000"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-53.733px; font-size:14pt" align=justify>Note 15: Fair Value Measurements (Continued)</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-53.733px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Loans held for sale</I> - Loans held for sale in the secondary market are carried at the lower of aggregate cost or estimated fair value. &nbsp;The fair value measurement of a loan held for sale is based on current secondary market prices for similar loans, which is considered a Level 2 measurement.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-53.733px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Loans</I> - Loans are not measured at fair value on a recurring basis. &nbsp;However, loans considered to be impaired (see Note 1) may be measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis. &nbsp;The fair value measurement of an impaired loan that is collateral dependent is based on the fair value of the underlying collateral. &nbsp;All other impaired loan measurements are based on the present value of expected future cash flows discounted at the applicable effective interest rate and, thus, are not fair value measurements. &nbsp;Fair value measurements of underlying collateral that utilize observable market data, such as independent appraisals reflecting recent comparable sales, are considered Level 2 measurements. &nbsp;Other fair value measurements that incorporate estimated assumptions market participants would use to measure fair value are considered Level 3 measurements.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Other real estate owned</I> - Real estate and other property acquired through or in lieu of loan foreclosure are not measured at fair value on a recurring basis.&nbsp; However, foreclosed assets are initially measured at fair value (less estimated costs to sell) when they are acquired and may also be measured at fair value (less estimated costs to sell) if they become subsequently impaired.&nbsp; The fair value measurement for each asset may be obtained from an independent firm or prepared internally.&nbsp; Fair value measurements obtained from independent firms are generally based on sales of comparable assets and other observable market data and are considered Level 2 measurements.&nbsp; Fair value measurements prepared internally are based on observable market data but include significant unobservable data and are therefore considered Level 3 measurements.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-42px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Loans with a carrying amount of $2,177,440 were considered impaired and were written down to their fair value of $1,892,440. &nbsp;As a result, the Company recognized a specific valuation allowance against these impaired loans totaling $285,000 during the year ended December 31, 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-42px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Other real estate owned with a carrying amount of $1,042,200 was written down to a fair value of $1,020,000. &nbsp;As a result, an impairment charge of $22,200 was included in earnings for the year ended December 31, 2011.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-42px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Company estimates fair value of all financial instruments regardless of whether such instruments are measured at fair value. &nbsp;The following methods and assumptions were used by the Bank to estimate fair value of financial instruments not previously discussed.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-42px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Cash and cash equivalents</I> - Fair value approximates the carrying value.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:14pt" align=justify>Note 15: Fair Value Measurements (Continued)</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Loans</I> - Fair value of variable rate loans that reprice frequently is based on carrying value. &nbsp;Fair value of other loans is estimated by discounting future cash flows using current rates at which similar loans would be made to borrowers with similar credit ratings. &nbsp;Fair value of impaired and other nonperforming loans is estimated using discounted expected future cash flows or the fair value of underlying collateral, if applicable.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Accrued interest receivable and payable</I> - Fair value approximates the carrying value</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Deposits</I> - Fair value of deposits with no stated maturity, such as demand deposits, savings, and money market accounts, by definition, is the amount payable on demand on the reporting date. &nbsp;Fair value of fixed rate time deposits is estimated using discounted cash flows applying interest rates currently being offered on similar time deposits.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Borrowed funds</I> &#150; Fair value of existing debt approximates the carrying value.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:14pt">Note 15: Fair Value Measurements (Continued)</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Limitations</I> - The fair value of a financial instrument is the current amount that would be exchanged between market participants, other than in a forced liquidation. &nbsp;Fair value is best determined based upon quoted market prices. &nbsp;However, in many instances, there are no quoted market prices for the Company's various financial instruments. &nbsp;In cases where quoted market prices are not available, fair values are based on estimates using present value or other valuation techniques. &nbsp;Those techniques are significantly affected by the assumptions used, including the discount rate and estimates of future cash flows. &nbsp;Accordingly, the fair value estimates may not be realized in an immediate settlement of the instrument. &nbsp;Consequently, the aggregate fair value amounts presented may not necessarily represent the underlying fair value of the Company.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:-54px; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Fair value estimates are made at a specific point in time based on relevant market information and information about the financial instrument. &nbsp;These estimates do not reflect any premium or discount that could result from offering for sale at one time the Company's entire holdings of a particular instrument. &nbsp;Because no market exists for a significant portion of the Company's financial instruments, fair value estimates are based on judgments regarding future expected loss experience, current economic conditions, risk characteristics of various financial instruments, and other factors. &nbsp;These estimates are subjective in nature and involve uncertainties and matters that could affect the estimates. &nbsp;Fair value estimates are based on existing on- and off-balance-sheet financial instruments without attempting to estimate the value of anticipated future business. &nbsp;Deposits with no stated maturities are defined as having a fair value equivalent to the amount payable on demand. &nbsp;This prohibits adjusting fair value derived from retaining those deposits for an expected future period of time. &nbsp;This component, commonly referred to as a deposit base intangible, is neither considered in the above amounts nor is it recorded as an intangible asset on the balance sheets. &nbsp;In addition, the tax ramifications related to the realization of the unrealized gains and losses can have a significant effect on fair value estimates and have not been considered in the estimates.</P>
